utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd first like to establish that the situation as far as Mr. Stanisic is present is concerned is the same as last time. The Chamber has received the non-attendance in court form. It's -- the report is the same as it was last time. We further have received yesterday's medical report by Dr. Eekhof, and as far as the Chamber understands, none of the parties have any questions for Dr. Eekhof, and since the Chamber has also no questions for Dr. Eekhof, we could proceed and we intend to proceed on the basis of what is written in that report, that is sessions of five quarters of an hour, then half an hour break, and all that total of five hours, not more. Then could we just verify whether the videolink is working properly. Mr. Stanisic, can you hear me, and can you see me? THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanisic. I take it that the telephone line with Mr. Knoops is functioning as well. If there would be any problem in communicating with Mr. Knoops, please inform the Chamber through the microphone. As far as the scheduling is concerned, we hopefully will complete Mr. Miljanic's testimony today. We'll hear the testimony of a witness who will testify under the pseudonym either later today and/or tomorrow. Then next week, the 14th of December, and perhaps some of the 15th of December, we'll hear the witness -- the testimony of Witness B-1058, and finally on Tuesday the 15th of December we'll hear the evidence of Witness B-1108. The Chamber was informed that the redactions were made in relation to the Exhibit D5. The redactions were made in both versions on e-court, and the Prosecution is invited to upload an unredacted version of the statement which would then be admitted under seal. Could you confirm, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. The Chamber received a request for provisional release from the Stanisic Defence. Mr. Groome, the Chamber would like to receive a response rather soon. When do you think you could --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We may have it today, Your Honour, if not tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That at least would mean that not by the mere fact that alleged response was there that the whole matter would be frustrated, so the Chamber will then consider the application and your response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's one more matter. In the decision delivered by the Chamber on the 3rd of November in which the provisional release of Mr. Stanisic was denied, the Chamber noted that it would follow up on the appropriateness of the direct contacts of the Stanisic Defence with the court's reporting medical officer, Dr. Eekhof. The Chamber would like to invite any interested party in this case, of course most likely the Stanisic Defence and the Prosecution, to submit written submissions in relation to this issue by the end of this week in they wish to do so. These were the procedural matters, and I would like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, Mr. Miljanic, unless there's -- may I take it on the basis of the time you've used with Mr. Miljanic up to this time, Mr. Weber, that I think it was scheduled for one hour and a half in chief, and we have used now approximately -- a little bit over half an hour. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My understanding is that 36 minutes have been used and 54 would remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I would call just a bit over half an hour. I understand your answer to be that you expect to stay within those limits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. No other matter then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony last week is still binding. That means that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Weber, will now continue his examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Last week you were discussing the commencement of the tank and artillery attack on Skabrnja at approximately 7.30 in the morning. How long did this artillery attack last on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't stop all -- all day on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where was the artillery fire landing in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the entire village and the surrounding villages with Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please address the areas within Skabrnja. Could you please describe the type of buildings located in the eastern and western parts of the village.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire village of Skabrnja was without any economic facilities or military facilities. The only facility with any economic significance was an agricultural co-operative. Then there was a church, the co-operative school, the clinic, and nothing else. All the rest were agricultural facilities, that is, farms, and there were also residential buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to these farms and residential buildings, where in Skabrnja were they located?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From one end of the village to the other. Actually, it was all mixed. There was no industrial zone or anything like that. The farms were family farms. They belonged to the families that lived in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the church, co-operative school, and clinic, were these buildings located within the centre of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre. And they are still there today, restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what was the name of the church that was located in the centre of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the church of the Holy Virgin Mary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 2870, lines 1 through 9 of exhibit P96, you state: "I found out from the couriers who came to report to me that there was general chaos, that the tanks from Zemunik Gornje and Biljana were heading our way, and that's -- that was as far as I knew myself." How often were couriers reporting back to you on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A dozen times or so. I can't give you a precise number, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you state that, "tanks were heading our way," what direction did you learn that the tanks were coming?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the direction of Zemunik Gornje and from the direction of the Zemunik airfield. It's also known as the Zadar airport, but actually it's the Zemunik airfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were there any forces that were moving in behind these tanks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that before the attack of the tanks there was artillery fire, then the tanks came, and they were followed by infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how many infantry soldiers followed the tanks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you give an estimation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to make a personal estimate, I would say that there were about 1.000 infantry soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 2871, lines 14 and 15, of Exhibit P96, you state: "At that point I lost track of time and everything. At that point, planes started firing cluster bombs." At what point in time did planes start firing cluster bombs on Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning. There was several bombings, but it may have been around 10.00 or 11.00. I cannot tell precisely. That was the first bombing, and it was followed by three to four more waves of bombers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These three to four waves of bombings that followed, did they all occur on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first bombing of Skabrnja was on the 2nd of October, 1991, when the first cluster bombs were dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that. What I'm asking you is after the initial bombing on the 18th of November, you described that there were subsequent bombings. Did these subsequent bombings occur on the same day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. Three or four more. I'm not sure. I don't remember, but I think it was all on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What forces did these planes belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where were the planes targeting with these cluster bombs on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first -- the first bombs fell near the school, and the church followed, and the entire village centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The church that you're referring to, is that the one located in the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At approximately 11.00 in the morning, did you observe any helicopters involved in the attack against Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already said that about 1 kilometre from the centre of the village to the west helicopters were observed taking infantry to that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how many helicopters did you observe?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four helicopters, and there were four landings. I saw it through all the smoke, and there were no less than four helicopter landings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where were you when you observed these helicopter landings?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I was at Razovljeva Glavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did you see the helicopters land?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right beneath my house. It's a meadow called Jabuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What did you see when the helicopters landed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw people getting off the helicopters and immediately taking combat positions. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 24322, lines 23 to 25 of Exhibit P95, you describe these individuals as members of special forces, and you state: "They wore dark blue uniforms and berets, and they were getting out of helicopters. Three or four helicopters landed two or three times and soldiers got off." Were the dark blue uniforms solid in colour or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell. I wasn't close enough. I know that they were in dark uniforms, but I'm really not sure whether that dark colour was dark blue or black.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you able to determine whether or not the uniforms were camouflage?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't able to determine whether they were camouflage or plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how many soldiers disembarked from the helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each helicopter carries 40 men. That would add up to -- well, I never made the calculation, but probably a company of the usual strength at the time in accordance with the military establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you know that these soldiers were special forces?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could tell by their headgear. They wore berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a brief intervention, if I may. It seems that the witness is being led to a wrong reply, and it's based on the wrong quoting of the exhibit of P95. On page 24322, the witness was -- said the JNA special forces and several times over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any wrong quotation, you may invite the other party or address me so that I can invite the other party to literally quote. So if any summary or any way of referring to a statement or to transcript is inaccurate, then the other party's invited to do it literally. And you said 24322. Which line? Where do you find a wrong quotation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm referring to lines 15 and 19 on that page. The witness in his previous testimonies designated the forces as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What he said in his previous testimony is now for Mr. Weber to quote. I want all parties to refrain by -- when making objections to already indicate what they consider relevant, important, wrong, whatever. So if you say that Mr. Weber mischaracterizes what the witness said, you may say so, that he mischaracterizes, and you may point at the specific part of the testimony, and then Mr. Weber is invited to rephrase his question with an accurate quoting of what he refers to. You said --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I tried to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Lines 15 and 19. Mr. Weber, could you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have accurately phrased it. Lines 15 through 19 was a statement by a Prosecutor in the former proceedings. What I'm referring to is the actual statement of the witness in his prior testimony, which is what I've drawn the Court's attention to. And the question that was posed to the witness was. "What kind of special forces did you think they were at the time?" His answer references based on his former JNA experience, he thinks that they're: "Special forces or elite units judging by their uniforms, their appearance and subsequent activities. I think they were special units, probably a special unit," and he does not reference particularly JNA. So I've gone with the witness's description.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you're reading could you please slow down so that our interpreters and transcribers can do their job. Now, let me go back to what the initial question was. Yes. If you would ask the witness -- let me see. Until now you have asked him to describe, and you're now referring to the previous testimony. Let me just have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the question posed to the witness was on page 9, line 12, and it's a rephrase of what was asked of him in the Milosevic testimony, that being what -- what kind of special forces did this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- in the -- could you take me to the exact page and line where this was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The question posed immediately before the objection was on page 9, line 12. I asked: "How did you know that these soldiers were special forces?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the source for knowledge of special forces? Apparently the Milosevic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give me exact page and line so that we can verify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- line 20, through page 24324, line 6 would encompass the full answer, which I'm trying to now elicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the transcript of the Milosevic case, on the top of page 24324, indicates that the witness was explaining why he thought they were special forces. That's in evidence. Therefore, what is wrong with Mr. Weber asking further details as how he recognised them as special forces, whether that was a mistake or whether that was right, but at least that's the evidence. What remains of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with that. I merely think that for reasons of fairness toward the witness, the context should be laid out of what the witness is explaining. The witness is speaking about JNA special forces, and he never mentions anything else in his statement. That is the essence of my objection. My learned friend Mr. Weber is mentioning special forces without making it clear what kind of special forces he's referring to, and we have many statements by -- made by this witness, and he speaks only about one category. I will not take any more of the Court's time. I believe it is clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's particularly a matter to be raised in cross-examination, Mr. Petrovic. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How did you know that these individuals who disembarked the helicopters were special forces?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although much time has elapsed since, my knowledge is based on the -- on my being a member of the JNA for a long time, and I was also commander of a special forces unit of the JNA, so that as a former professional soldier, I was able to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How were you -- how were you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Special forces as opposed to regular JNA forces wore different headgear. All special forces wore berets, and regular soldiers and regular units wore the so-called Tito cap. That's one difference. And then there's another -- they also differed in weapons. Special forces also had special weapons and special equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Special weapons being what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had weapons with silencers, that is, automatic light weapons such as Heckler pistols at the time, or Uzis. Then grenade throwers, smoke grenades and other equipment, and silencers more specifically. They were also part of their standard equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These weapons that you just described, were these the types of weapons that were being carried by the special forces on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. That was obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Where did the special forces go after they disembarked the helicopters?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they moved towards the village of Skabrnja. That was, say, 4 or 500 metres away from the houses. They set out towards those houses in the settlement of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you learn what these soldiers did from these special forces once they reached the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day I found out a lot of things. Now, whether this was correct information or not is something that I cannot be sure of. However, the most terrible things happened. Killings. People, civilians were being dragged out of basements. There were killings, massacres. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, I know you've detailed the events of the 18th of November in your testimony in previous cases. What I have remaining are just a few general questions before discussing some exhibits. On page 4 of the English version of Exhibit P97, you reference that Skabrnja was attacked by at least a thousand soldiers as part of the "strategic action." And on page 2875, lines 19 through 21 of Exhibit P96, you state: "They wanted to trap the village completely and not to let anyone leave this place alive. That was the objective. We learned about this in the army. It's called 'Pliers'." Could you please explain what you meant in your statement by "strategic action."

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I meant: I meant that Skabrnja was not a regular tactical target. It was a strategic target with a view to intimidation, killing, and showing by way of an example what would happen to others, because Skabrnja was a purely Croat village. That's what I meant, that it was strategic. It was a politically strategic question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the military strategy being employed by the military forces attacking the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I hesitate, but still I question the competence of this witness as a lay-witness to go into a question of military strategics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, once we hear that he recognised this, then of course the next question would be what he then exactly recognized, and that will further enable us to see whether this is within the scope of what a witness of fact can tell us or whether it's beyond that scope. Please proceed. Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the question be repeated and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I rephrase it for you. What did you see or what did you observe which made you believe that this was the strategic action as you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because I saw that in this very small area there -- it was -- it was the fact that such forces were sent to deal with such a small number of people in such a very small area like that village. That's how I came to think that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What did you mean by "Pliers"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I studied that, and that's what I did for 23 years in the former JNA. That meant surrounding and destroying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How is the strategy employed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was deployed quite literally in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How was this done?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they used artillery pieces to bomb in order to soften or, rather, to intimidate people so that they would escape into basements, and then with the fast infantry and helicopters they surrounded the area and they dealt with these civilians and members of the reserve MUP force, et cetera, and they got them all out and killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After the 18th of November, 1991, did you have occasion to go to the pathology department in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly how many days after the 18th. I came to the pathology department when the dead bodies from Skabrnja were brought in, including my father, my brother, and seven relatives of mine. I came there to identify the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the witness please have Prosecution 65 ter 712. Actually, could we please have page 2 of both the B/C/S and English version of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is now being shown to you is an official record of Croatian soldiers and civilians who were killed. This document comes from the Zadar county, Skabrnja municipality dated 9 July 2002. Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to number 6, Vladimir Horvat. Do you know the profession of this individual?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know what Vladimir Horvat did. He was a waiter at the company in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know if he died on the 18th of November, 1991, and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how he died: He got out of Skabrnja during the 18th, but afterwards he returned to get his wife and two young children out. That's where they waited for him and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was he with anyone else at this time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with Nedeljko, Nedeljko Juric, Nedeljko Juric, and Perica Gaspar. They had returned to get their wives and children out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have page 3 in both the B/C/S and English versions of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to number 12, Slavko Miljanic. Is this a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my brother, Slavko Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was your brother's profession on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked at the furniture factory on the island of Preko near Zadar. He was a carpenter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he died on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His wife, my sister-in-law, told me about that. He had escaped into the field, and then he returned. He took his son, and they killed him while he held his son in his arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to number 14, Mile Pavicic. What was this individual's profession?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His father has some construction equipment, bulldozers and the like. He used to work with his father. He was a construction worker. He drove this machinery to places where they would work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he died on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I do. My mother told me about that. When they came to that basement, they took him and his father out, as well as all other males. They took them all out of that basement. There was no sound of shooting. Silencers were used -- a silencer was used by one single man who killed all of them, from age 20 to 85. I must add that based on the testimony of my mother and all the rest who were there, these people that killed them had masks on their faces, and they had silencers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you've already described number 16. I'd like to direct your attention to number 17, Ante Razov. What was Mr. Razov's profession in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a barber. He worked in Zadar at the barber shop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, again my mother saw what they did to him. He was caught alive. They were beating him and banging him on the asphalt road. My mother and the other women didn't know who these people were, but one of the members came there and put a gun and fired into his head, got a knife out, cut off his ear, wrapped it up and put it in his pocket, and then they threw him into the bushes. So he was still alive when thrown in there, and -- and he was dying for over an hour. So he suffered greatly. There were other women there who were witnesses to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have page 4 of the B/C/S and English versions of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to number 18, Marko Rogic. What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a salesperson. He is my next-door neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he died on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When my brother died, roughly. I don't know exactly, but it was in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to numbers 20 through 22. Are these individuals related?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twenty and 21 and 22, they're brothers, Bude, Ivica, and Milenko Segaric. They're three brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the professions of each of these brothers were.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bude Segaric was a worker, a construction worker. Ivica Segaric worked for the then company of Jugolinija on ships, so he was a sailor, and he had just come home a day before that. Miljenko worked at the Boris Kidric textile factory in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Apologies, Your Honour. Mr. Stanisic asked to be excused to use the men's room. Yes, we have no objection to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have agreed on that with Mr. Stanisic, then we will continue, and he's excused for the time being. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to Bude and Miljenko Segaric, do you know how they died on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. They were captured in Tomo Pavicic's basement. They were loaded onto a refrigerator truck, a truck for refrigerating meat together with some young boys, and they were taken to Benkovac. Five days later Ratko Mladic handed over their bodies to the Croatian side in Zitnic near Sibenik. I don't know how they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to number 21, Ivica Segaric, how did he die on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got killed in Pavicic's basement. He was with his wife and two children in the basement, and they dragged him out and killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to number 23, Sime Segaric, what was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sime Segaric worked in the Adria Fish Factory in Zadar. He was a worker, and he was late for work on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the man who came to tell me in the morning that tanks were coming in from Gornje Zemunik. I issued him the order to have everyone hide in cellars, basements, and I haven't seen him since. I don't know how he actually got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the witness could please have page 5 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to number 24, Nediljko Skara. What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think he was a construction worker. Well, I know very little about him because he doesn't come from my part of the village. He comes from a different part of the village. He wasn't very highly educated or anything like that. He was an ordinary worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he was killed in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard people from the village talking about it. I don't know whether it's correct or not. I guess it is. They captured him -- or, rather, killed him while he was trying to flee, and he was running by the railroad and that's where he was killed. I didn't see it, but that's what people say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to number 25 Stanko Vickovic. What was his profession?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a driver in the Jadran Construction Company. He's also a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how he died on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how he died. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to these individuals, in the B/C/S version of this document it refers to them as Branitelj. Could you please explain the differential between Branitelj and Vojak, in Croatian?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a major difference involved. Vojnik is a soldier, a person who has a soldier's uniform, soldier's equipment and weapons. Branitelj is a defender who can be a member of the civilian protection. I have to say that at that time we based all of this on what used to be done in the former JNA, so they were what was known as members of the civilian protection. They and their families were supposed to be given some compensation because they had nothing. The Croatian state registered them as defenders so that they would give pensions to their wives and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to ask you about one individual under the list of civilians on this same page. If I could direct your attention to number 3, Luka Bilaver. Do you know how this individuals -- strike that -- what condition he was in on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although he was a neighbour of mine, I hadn't seen him for a long time, because he was an old man who was bedridden because he had had a stroke. I had not seen him for over a month when I come from Zadar to Skabrnja and things like that. However, I always asked the members of his family how he was doing, and they would tell me that he was bedridden. And that's how he was before the 18th and on the eve of the 18th. I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him alive after the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that even before the 18th I certainly hadn't seen him in about a month. I did not see him alive then or a month before that or afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders Prosecution 65 ter 712. The Stanisic Defence has already indicated that they have no objection to its admission. I do not know about the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit P99, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P99 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of Exhibit P97, you indicate that you reviewed photographs and you recognise a number of individuals depicted in these photographs. Sir, did you have occasion to review Prosecution 65 ter 2811 prior to your testimony, and is this exhibit a photo album that is referenced in Exhibit P97, your ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is depicted in the photographs in this album?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dead bodies of my fellow villagers from Skabrnja in front of their houses and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were these individuals killed on the 18th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Probably. I did not see that, only in photographs, but on the basis of what people told me -- well, as I've said, I did not see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, but did you recognise these individuals as people that were killed that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I not recognise them? All of them are my neighbours, relatives, and friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are any of the individuals depicted in these photographs armed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 2811, again without any objection from the Stanisic Defence. I do not know from the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit P100, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P100 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber, is there any reason why we didn't see it on our screens or -- when you refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There are a lot of photos in this photo album. They are of a very graphic nature. They do have a forensic purpose. They include photographs of the relatives of this witness. At this time, due to the efficiency of the proceedings, he's described them in his statement, and we're tendering them in bulk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would I be surprised the witness to know whether this is 65 ter 2811 or anything else. If only the cover would be shown, then at least we'd know what we're talking about. I don't think that under the present circumstance that it causes any major problems, but as a rule, I'd like to see on the screen, not necessarily to be done now, but as a rule I'd like to see on the screen what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. In the future I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, P100 is admitted into evidence. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The only remaining series of questions related to a second photo album and then I was going to tender that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, did you have occasion to view a second photo album that depicted various locations in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is depicted in the photographs of these locations in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main road of Skabrnja and houses. They are all houses in the neighbourhood of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do these photographs depict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, again, why not, if only one or just the cover page of that photo album on the screen so that apart from you and the witness, the triers of fact also know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could please have page 2 of 65 ter 2812.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the church in Skabrnja demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What church?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The church of the Holy Virgin Mary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could I please have page 13 of this exhibit, the lower left-hand photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the main road that goes through the village of Skabrnja and the surrounding houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1991, what did you see occurring on this road?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, one second. When you are referring to pages, are you referring to e-court pages or to any other pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I've been referring to the e-court page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- for page 13 out of 18, I have four small photographs on one page. That's the one I have on my screen for page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct. There are four photographs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're showing the left bottom photograph on page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1991, what did you see occurring on this road?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the stretch of road right before the village centre, and tanks were driving down the road, four tanks, actually, in combat formation, and they had civilians as a human shield in front of them, women, children, and elderly people. About 200 civilians were walking in front of the tanks. And not only in front but also on the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have the entire page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the other locations that are depicted on this page?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the very centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And does -- do these photographs accurately depict destruction that was done to the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Have you had occasion to also view the other photographs that are contained in this album?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do these other photographs also accurately depict the destruction that was done to the village of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 2812 into evidence, again with no objection from the Stanisic Defence. I do not know about the Simatovic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I ask Madam Registrar to assign a number, could you tell us when these photographs were taken, by whom, and who selected them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These photographs come from a collection of -- that were -- they relate to -- another witness will be offering descriptions of this. This witness's knowledge, I believe he's testified to and that's the scope of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't aware that another witness would explain to us who took them and when they were taken, but if we hear that evidence at a later stage, that's fine. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will become Exhibit P101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P101 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Just so it's clear for the record, what I was showing in court is page 13 in e-court, which is also page 13 of now Exhibit 101.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I was so busy trying to find it on my screen that I missed that you had already indicated that it was the lower left photograph of that page 13. So there was no need to ask it any further. Apologies for that. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Then we'll first have a break. We will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will it be the Stanisic Defence or the Simatovic Defence who cross-examines the witness first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, you will be cross-examined now by Mr. Knoops. Mr. Knoops is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, first of all, we would like to express our appreciation for testifying here today despite the difficult circumstances you -- you have faced. Mr. Miljanic, do you agree that the attack by the JNA was purely a military operation by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you please explain us why you can't answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no military targets in Skabrnja, no military targets at all there. So I don't know what it's about then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, can you recall that in your very first statement in 1996 you -- you gave a name to the JNA operation in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I may have though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In that statement of 1996, you mentioned that it was JNA military operation, the so-called strategic action. Can you recall making that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I think I did make that statement, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us on the basis of what knowledge you were able to qualify that operation as strategic action?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's based on the following facts, and I as a former professional soldier know that: If it had been a tactical action, and tactics is a lower level than strategy, then there would have been much less military materiel, fewer armaments, and fewer soldiers. So judging by the scope of military capabilities used, I concluded that this was a strategic action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So the term "strategic action" was not an official term. It was a term you gave to that action, that operation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, do you agree that this strategic action, as you mention it, was actually conducted under command and control of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you see yourself any of the military commanders of the JNA in charge of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you at a certain point during this operation you overheard a conversation between JNA commanders?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of the JNA commanders of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic, who then was a JNA colonel; and Colonel Cecovic, the commander -- a brigade commander from Benkovac whom I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that according to your knowledge, a motorised brigade from the JNA was involved in this operation, this strategic operation you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that at a certain point that brigade was in need of reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that those reinforcements were at that point supplied by the JNA itself?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know who sent reinforcements. I wasn't in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you overheard a conversation between Lieutenant-Colonel Sekovic and Mr. Vladic whereby the latter promised him, Sekovic, to provide ammunition and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree that considering the strength of the JNA at that time, you estimated it around a thousand soldiers, that the attack was actually conducted by means of overkill of JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there was no need for the JNA to have other forces, satellite units, external forces, being there to support the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the number of soldiers, I personally think that they didn't need any other forces, but I don't know. I think they had enough soldiers, actually even too many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, you testified about the presence of special forces. Is it correct that these special forces belonged to a parachute unit from Nis?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my line of thinking at the time based on my knowledge of the situation, but whether or not they really were from Nis I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And does this knowledge extend to the -- all the helicopter landings you mentioned? You mentioned four helicopter landings, unloading each 40 soldiers. Is it your understanding that all of these soldiers were from the parachute unit Nis?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a helicopter can carry 40 soldiers, so if you add that up, knowing the number of helicopters, you can make your own calculation. I really don't know who was involved. I cannot really precisely identify the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Were you able to discover what colour of military hats these -- this unit wore? I refer to the units which were unloaded from the helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw that they were berets, but I couldn't tell the colour because the distance was about a kilometre. So I couldn't really tell the colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, do you agree that those special forces can be qualified as infantry?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Knowing their role, that's a way of defining them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And it is your understanding that this infantry belonged to the JNA in terms of command and control; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Calls for a legal conclusion and it's speculation at this time without listing the basis of knowledge that he would have for this question or answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would think that you need a lot of questions, factual questions, to rephrase the matter, but I leave it to you and carefully listen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, did you at that time have any knowledge onto which army those special forces belonged?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you later learn about any relationship, if any, between those special forces and any army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Afterward, I found out, a few days later. In a conversation I learned how civilians were killed, that they were killed, in accordance with my knowledge, and they were killed by masked people with painted faces, who had weapons with silencers, but that's what I learned subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, I come to that point later if I may. My question is to you: Did you later learn whether there was any relationship between those special forces which landed through the helicopters and any army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't learn anything about that. Who their leader was, what their role was, I never found that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, I'm just -- and I'm also looking at you, Mr. Weber. Is there any dispute about who could use helicopters at that time under those circumstances? If there's a dispute about it, then of course it's a matter to -- first of all, to explore what kind of helicopters these were. I'm just addressing you before --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In my view there can be no dispute that at that time only the JNA was able to have helicopters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Because I tried to understand your line of questioning, Mr. Knoops. If 40 people come out of a helicopter, which you say must be a JNA helicopter, then apart from whether you explore what kind of link there is, then to ask was there any link with an army, then I would say at least they were on board of a helicopter which belonged to a JNA army, whatever the witness says. So, therefore, I'm asking myself what the testimony is -- what the questioning is heading for. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was -- my -- the basis of my question was, of course, was -- were these special forces under command and control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: There was an objection. The Court invited me to lay a foundation for coming to this very question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If the Prosecution has no dispute about these helicopters being part of the JNA, I don't see the objection anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, command and control -- I mean, you can transport people without being fully in command of control of the OC [phoen]. You can provide services, but your question was, is there any relation with any army, at least a relation which seems to be not in dispute is that they were on board helicopters belonging to an army, and the parties agree on that. So I would then expect you to say, do you know anything about how they got into the helicopters, who was on board of the helicopter, because -- instead of saying, is there any link with an army -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to -- yes, Mr. Weber, may I take it that you did not in any way dispute that these were JNA helicopters or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a matter that's in dispute, so I'm sorry for cutting you off there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's not in dispute, I believe that the JNA had involvement in this attack, and there was co-ordination amongst units including the JNA in this attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Helicopters were not JNA in your -- I'm talking about helicopters having 40 people on board, whether these were JNA helicopters. If that's in dispute, fine. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I think I'm a bit more familiar with this. There will be evidence led in this case that the unit, the Red Berets, on some occasions used JNA helicopters and on other occasions used their own helicopters. So they were in possession of their own helicopters, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Big ones containing 40 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't know off the top of my head, Your Honour, how many people would fit in them, but I'm not sure. It's -- I'm not sure it's a resolved matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we therefore should ask about what kind of helicopters we're dealing with. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just an observation. The Court, I believe, last week intervened by saying that the counsel who was not examining or cross-examining the witness cannot be supported by the co-counsel. Just observe that the -- or the counsel of the Prosecution is at least supporting one of the objections of the leading counsel. We believe that the Court should then allow also the Defence counsel to, if necessary, support leading counsel in the examination or cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there are two different matters. The first is putting questions to the witness and to consult with co-counsel or being advised by co-counsel. I have no recollection that I ever in this case or any other case prevented counsel from consulting each other on matters. It's a different matter, but I'm not going make a lot of problems about it. It's certainly highly uncommon that where one counsel examines a witness that the other one also then jumps in without any further explanation, whereas consulting between counsel or answering questions from the Bench, which are not questions to a witness, seeking certain information, if their one counsel says, "I'm better acquainted with the matter than my colleague," under those circumstances I think it's appropriate that other counsel takes over, and I want to clearly distinguish between the two situations. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, were you able to identify the type of helicopters you mentioned, the four helicopters which unloaded the 40 special forces units?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what type of helicopters you -- you saw.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MI-8, Soviet made. These are helicopters that I personally flew on on many occasions. That's how I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And am I correct by saying that these helicopters were used by the JNA at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Witness, till what time, what year those helicopters were used by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the time. To the present day they are being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you ever, Mr. Witness, see that type of helicopter being used by other military forces than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used by the Croatian Army afterwards when it was armed. They used those very same helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you ever see those helicopters being used by paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used by the MUP. I don't know about paramilitaries, what they used. In Croatia it was only the MUP, and I don't know about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Referring to MUP, you -- you referred to MUP Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The MUP of Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that the helicopters which were landed and described you -- belonged to the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You testified that these special forces were directed to certain areas in the city. Do you have any information, direct knowledge, or information afterwards, which led you to the conclusion that these special forces were under supervision of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that personally. I personally did not see that, but on the basis of what I learn later -- I don't have any personal knowledge, but during conversations with all these people who were in the village -- well, I wouldn't want to go into that now, not unless it's absolutely necessary, but these people who told me about it know about this. I do not have any direct knowledge, because if I had knowledge of that, I probably would not be here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, is it correct that apart from the soldiers of the JNA and these special forces, also local people were involved in the crimes you described?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Who were these people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Local people from the villages around that area wearing JNA uniforms. They were there too. I repeat once again: I did not see it myself. I'm saying this on the basis of what my family told me, what my mother told me, what my friends told me. They knew these people very well. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the family members who told you so are able to give you names of the local people who supported the JNA at that time in JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every one of these persons has his or her own version, and I don't know who to trust. As for the deaths of my nearest and dearest, I have at least ten versions, and I did not see that. So it involves the death of my father, too, and I really wouldn't want to be involved in guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, is it correct that there were residents from the municipality of Zemunik Gornje involved in the attack?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat once again: On the basis of what survivors said. I did not see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But did you hear from those survivors that residents were involved in the attacks from the municipality of Zemunik Gornje? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct that residents were involved in the attack from the village of Nadin, N-a-d-i-n?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the village of Nadin, on the very next day after Skabrnja, it was destroyed. I don't know if there were any Serbs in Nadin. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Did you hear from survivors that residents of that village were involved in the attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Nadin very well, but the village behind Nadin -- well, people talked about some people, but I didn't see that myself. I heard about it, though, but I did not see it myself. I don't have any direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Miljanic, in the 2003 statement you mentioned the involvement, apart from the JNA, of paramilitaries. Can you recall giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you have said that the village of Skabrnja fell into the hands of the JNA and paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just please have a follow-up question on that. I was going to object to the form of the question. It's a bit vague in terms of what it's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, I refer to the statement. I cannot make it more precise because that's in the statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the literal language the witness used, then it's fair to put the question to him if it, however, rephrases or summarises then on the basis your objection it should be literally quoted. I have not checked yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was just noting it because there's a time reference before in the phrasing of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean whether it refers to the 18th or an earlier date. Mr. -- could you give that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The statement of the witness, 19 June 2003. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think the time-frame Mr. Weber is seeking for is about Skabrnja to fall in the hands of the JNA. I take it that you're talking about the 18th of November. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't specify. The statement is: "Before Skabrnja fell into the hands of the JNA and the paramilitary units, one of the houses had been entirely destroyed by a cluster bomb." That's in the first paragraph of the 2003 statement, without time reference, I'm sorry, but this what's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's before Skabrnja fell into the hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection on the basis of whether or not the Stanisic Defence is accurately quoting it, just -- I believe the way the question was formed in and of itself it is vague as opposed to the time reference that was particularly now referenced for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the appropriate question would be, "When you said in your statement this and this and this, what time-frame did you have in mind?" If you would please explore this, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your 2003 statement it's been said: "Before Skabrnja fell into the hands of the JNA and paramilitary units, one of the houses had been entirely destroyed by cluster bombs." What time reference you had in mind when you gave this statement to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th, the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljanic. Is it correct that when you referred to the paramilitary units in this statement, you're actually referring to the local individuals who supported the JNA in the attacks as mentioned by you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mean the locals only. I also meant those who had fled, that is to say the policemen who had joined the then project that was underway, namely policemen, members of the different units that had been established at the time. So it's not only the JNA, and it's not only from the neighbouring villages. There were also paramilitary formations, and there was the police. They were -- the police were a paramilitary formation at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So please tell us what are exactly the paramilitary formations or units you refer to in your 2003 statement.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was the legal army, the legal army. It was the active legal army. All the rest were paramilitary formations. These were different volunteer units, then the local population, the forces of the then SUP. So these were groups of people who were not part of the JNA. All the rest were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And the elements of local populations, forces of the SUP, volunteer units, and police units, did you see yourself that they were part of this paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see this myself. It was only on television, only on television then. And also, I heard it in conversations, because I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia, so I did have some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: When was it then you -- that you saw on television that these formations were part of the paramilitary unit you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on television, before that I saw -- well, quite simply even during 1991 I saw Mr. Martic and all the rest, all the rest who stated publicly on television what they would do and so on. So it was no secret. It was on television every day in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, do you recall that in the Martic trial you testified that you were not able to define the name of the paramilitary unit and that you did not know about the composition of them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in that trial you were asked also about the paramilitary units, and you told the Court that these were Chetniks? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that anymore. Perhaps I did say it, but I don't remember anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that if you testified in the Martic case that these paramilitaries were referred to as Chetniks, would you agree to me that this was your testimony in the Martic case, or do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could have a line and page reference, maybe this is a matter that whether or not he actually said it in his testimony would be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It's page 2918, line 11 and lines 22 till 25, running to page 2919, lines 1 till 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Counsel, am I correct in you're referring to Judge Moloto's question as just before we went to the break you said that these paramilitaries were referred to as Chetniks? Is that how that's starting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. And it starts at line 11 -- 10, 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm clear on the reference. The only objection that the Prosecution would have is that the question that was phrased to the witness was that he was calling them Chetniks. I believe it's clear from his testimony that others were calling them that. I believe that the question should reflect the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is it correct that you testified in the Martic case that you learned from other individuals that those paramilitary formations were referred to as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Miljanic, that those Chetniks were predominantly local Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could you place -- please explain why that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because quite simply at the time on television and everywhere else there were these Chetniks. They introduced themselves. They said where they came from, from which particular place in the former Yugoslavia. They introduced themselves. They sang. They danced the Kolo. All sorts of things. Some of them were bragging about the fact that they were from a particular part of Serbia, those from Bosnia, et cetera, so I came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But what you learned from the survivors is that there were local Chetniks involved.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that as well. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it correct that it was your understanding at that moment that those local Chetniks were organised?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably someone had organised them. It's not that they came of their own free accord. That would be so unclear to me that a group of people would get together and just randomly go to a particular place. Someone must have organised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you know who organised them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether those Chetniks - you learned later from people that they were referred to as Chetniks - whether those Chetniks wore emblems?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we saw that every day on television. We saw it on television every day, Chetnik emblems. I mean, I really don't know how I would answer this question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: What do you mean with "Chetnik emblems"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these people were mostly unkempt, unshaven. They had long beards. They had these black caps, and on them was the Chetnik emblem, the Serbian eagle. That was the emblem of the Chetniks. That was no secret. It was a public matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And is it correct that those Chetniks had black faces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, I beg your pardon. Just a brief intervention. I'm sorry for interrupting. Just a brief intervention with regard to the transcript. Page 45, line 14. The witness said Subara, whereas here it says black caps. That could be relevant for understanding the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you're not supposed to tell us what the witness said. You can say, Could we verify that line. That's the way in which -- then we ask the witness, "After you said they had long beards, could you please repeat what you then said," because what I want to avoid at any cost is that the parties are telling not only the Court but also the witness what he said, how it has to be translated, where it went wrong. Therefore, again you're perfectly entitled to seek verification of something, but it should be done in the way as I just said. So therefore then you say there may be a translation error. May I take you to page so-and-so, line so-and-so, and then we'll verify that without already telling the witness what he's supposed to have said or what the interpreters should have told us. That's the neutral way in approaching these matters. I spent a bit more time on it now because that's what I expect the parties to do. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution just wanted to note that the question posed at page 45, line 18, which is the question that's pending, is vague in terms of what's referenced in terms of "black faces." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, let's take matters one by one. First, one of your answers, Mr. Miljanic, was that those persons are unkempt, unshaven. They had long beards, and then you said something in addition to that. What did you then tell? What did you then say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That they wore caps. They wore black caps. That is a form. I mean in our part of the world, in the Balkans. It's called Subara. And also there are the caps called Sajkaca. So there were the Subara-type caps and the Sajkaca caps. They are two different types, but what matters is the emblem on the cap. That is the eagle with four --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the last word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
